Aspirated kappa with long eta and acute/circumflex [kʰɛ̌ː], the pitch peak and the core meaning 'beginning, rule, first principle'.

pronunciation.approximation: 'ar-KHAY' — the second syllable is long, pitched high, and begins with a breathy 'kh'.

pronunciation.note: Archḗ is Tier 1 because the Greek ἀρχή contains both length (η) and stress (acute/circumflex) on the same syllable. The word is foundational for Greek philosophy, political theory, and theology.

domains.title: The First Principle
domains.subtitle: Origin, Rule, Sovereignty
domains.lead: Archḗ is the Greek word for beginning, origin, and rule. For philosophers it names the first principle from which all things derive; for political thinkers it names legitimate authority. It is a concept so central that Western thought still builds on it.

cards.name: First Principle
cards.desc: For the Presocratics, the archē is water, air, fire, or the boundless from which all things come.

cards.name: Rule and Authority
cards.desc: The same word means 'rule' or 'office'; origin and authority are inseparable in Greek.

cards.name: Cosmogonic Source
cards.desc: In Orphic and Neoplatonic thought, archē names the ultimate source of the cosmos.

cards.name: Foundation
cards.desc: Every discipline seeks its archē: the axiom, cause, or origin from which it proceeds.

symbols.name: Cornerstone

symbols.meaning: The symbol of rule derived from primordial authority

mythology.lead: Archḗ has no traditional mythology. Its stories are philosophical: the search by Greek thinkers for the first thing, the ruling thing, the thing from which everything else can be understood.

myths.title: Water as Arche
myths.text: Thales of Miletus declared that water (hydōr) is the archē of all things. Living things need water; land floats on water; water can become solid, liquid, and vaporous. His claim launched Western philosophy by asking not what things are made of but what they come from.

myths.title: The Boundless
myths.text: Anaximander argued that the archē cannot be any one element like water, since opposites must be generated from something neutral. He called it the apeiron, the boundless or indefinite, from which all things arise and to which they return by necessity.

myths.title: The Four Causes
myths.text: Aristotle organized the search for archē into four causes: material, formal, efficient, and final. To know a thing is to know its archai. This framework dominated Western science and metaphysics until the scientific revolution.

lore.syncretism: Archḗ entered Latin as principium and regula, and through Christian theology as 'principium' and 'archē' applied to Christ (John 1:1 uses archē). In modern English it survives in 'archaic,' 'architect,' 'anarchy,' and 'monarchy.' The philosophical quest for a first principle continues in physics (the theory of everything), mathematics (axioms), and biology (the origin of life).
lore.culturalLegacy: Archḗ is the word behind every search for origins. Archaeology, architecture, archives, and anarchy all carry its root. The concept shapes how Western culture thinks about authority: legitimate rule must derive from a valid beginning. To restore archḗ in Unicode is to restore the question from which philosophy begins.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Archḗ is the question that never stops being asked. What comes first? What rules? What makes everything else possible? Every civilization answers differently — water, fire, air, God, energy, information — but the form of the question is Greek.

The double meaning of archē — beginning and rule — is itself a wisdom. To begin something is to establish authority over it. The founder of a city, the first principle of a science, the opening sentence of a story: all are archai. The word thus invites us to examine our own beginnings, for they determine the shape of everything that follows.

sources.name: Kirk, Raven, and Schofield, The Presocratic Philosophers

lore.archaeology: Archḗ has no material cult. Its archaeological trace is the library: the papyri and manuscripts in which Greek philosophers asked after first principles. The word appears on inscriptions describing offices and origins, but the concept itself belongs to the history of ideas rather than to temple archaeology.
